slides.title: Estate cost and data-product decision pack

scqa: The census measured 638 of 1006 tables and 351.3 GiB of data and index. Separate enumerations of object and file stores were priced at reference list prices, not the owner's invoice.

Database reclaim is only 15.2 GiB, or 4.3% of bytes. Meanwhile 23.0% of rows are degraded, 81.7% have empty required-looking fields and 71.8% of sampled rows carry personal-data markers. Rights are declared, not measured.
Which cost strategies and which of the 8 product candidates should the owner take forward, and which should wait?

Take forward the archive-class move and the duplicate-object check as verified proposals; priced strategies total 1,174.4 USD a month. Defer database housekeeping and every product release until rights and de-identification are settled.

slides.title: Three strategies reach 100.0% of addressable bytes, almost all in object stores

points: The census measured 638 of 1006 tables, so database totals rest on partial coverage.
The estate holds 351.3 GiB of data and index; 350.3 GiB sits in the largest databases, which is 99.7% of the total.
Only 15.2 GiB is reclaimable in the databases before pricing, which is 4.3% of their bytes.
Dead columns are 13.0% of measured columns, which is a tidying task rather than a material saving.
slides.title: Database bytes are concentrated and little of them is reclaimable

points: Exact duplicate rows are 1.5% of rows, and reclaimable bytes are 4.3%; deduplication alone will not change the cost picture.
Degraded rows are 23.0%, which limits the value of any dataset built from them without cleansing first.
Rows with empty required-looking fields are 81.7%; the label is a heuristic, so treat it as a completeness warning, not a count of faults.
Sampled rows carrying personal-data markers are 71.8%; absence of a marker is not absence of personal data.
slides.title: Quality and exposure problems dwarf duplication in the measured rows

points: Personal-data markers were checked on 1.0m million sampled rows, so the 71.8% figure is a sample estimate.
Bytes not written for over a year are 15.4% of the total, which makes them candidates for cold storage.
There are 71 duplicate table pairs; some may be deliberate staging or backup copies, so confirm ownership before retiring any.
There are 368 empty tables out of 1006; a freshly truncated live table looks the same, so check before dropping.
slides.title: Stale bytes, duplicate pairs and empty tables give a tidy-up list, not a large saving

slides.title: The three priced strategies differ widely in saving and in how certain it is

points: First, check read frequency before archiving old buckets; 986.5 USD a month, before retrieval fees.
Second, confirm duplicate objects by content hash before deleting; 180.3 USD a month is an estimate.
Third, defer database tidying: cold tables save 5.9 USD a month, all reclaim 15.2 GiB.
Fourth, release nothing until rights are bound; markers sit in 71.8% of sampled rows.
slides.title: Verify the two object-store moves first; defer database tidying and every release

points: Sampled ratios, such as 1.5% and 81.7%, are estimates until a complete-pass census runs.
Rights and licences are unmeasured; none of the 8 candidates is releasable until rights are bound.
The artists_app connection could not be read pending a MySQL grant, and 638 of 1006 tables were measured.
Some buckets were unreachable and file-share duplication is unknown; prices are list, not invoice.
